summaries.example: Think about a coral reef. A tiny coral polyp is clearly a living individual. But a whole reef is made from many polyps, algae, and hard deposits. The reef can grow and be damaged, so we may ask whether it is one living individual, a group of individuals, or both. The answer depends on what we are trying to explain.
summaries.summary: The entry asks a basic but difficult question: what counts as a biological individual? Common examples include animals, plants, and mushrooms, but biology also contains less obvious cases. A huge fungus may spread across a wide area while remaining genetically connected. A coral reef includes many polyps, algae, and nonliving deposits, yet the reef can grow and depend on the coordinated activity of its parts. These cases show that nature does not always provide a clear label saying “one individual.” Philosophers and biologists study several features that might help: physical boundaries, cooperation among parts, metabolism, growth, reproduction, and control. Some individuals are important because they can take part in evolution; others are important because their parts form a working living whole. The entry therefore considers more than one kind of individuality. It also examines microbes, partnerships between species, groups such as insect colonies, and larger lineages. Its central lesson is that the best answer may depend on the biological question being asked.
key_ideas: Biological individuals are not always just familiar animals and plants. They can also be tiny parts, large groups, or collections of different living things.
Scientists and philosophers disagree about where one individual ends and another begins.
An organism is one important kind of biological individual, but the two ideas may not mean exactly the same thing.
Biological individuality can involve working together, having a boundary, using energy, growing, or taking part in reproduction.
Different questions may call for different ways of counting biological individuals.
summaries.why_it_matters: Knowing what counts as one living individual helps us understand bodies, microbes, ecosystems, reproduction, and evolution. It also reminds us that simple everyday categories do not always fit the living world. Careful counting and clear definitions can help scientists describe complicated partnerships without pretending that every case has one obvious answer.

important_terms.definition: A living thing, part, or group that can be counted as one biological unit for some purpose.
A living thing made of parts that work together as a whole, such as a tree or an animal.
The way a living thing uses materials and energy to keep working.
A close relationship in which different kinds of living things live together and affect one another.
The ability of a living thing or group to control some of its own activities.

questions_to_think_about: Is a coral reef one individual, many individuals, or both?
What makes the parts of a living thing work together?
Could a group of animals ever act like one larger living thing?
Should we count a tiny living part, such as a bacterium, as an individual?

summaries.example: A Hawaiian bobtail squid lives with Vibrio bacteria that help it function. One question is whether the squid and bacteria form a physiological individual: their activities are tightly integrated, and the partnership helps the squid operate. A different question asks whether the squid-bacteria complex is an evolutionary or Darwinian individual. That requires considering whether the complex forms the right kind of parent-offspring lineage, with heritable variation affecting reproduction. The same complex can therefore look unified in one framework but not qualify as an evolutionary individual in another.
summaries.summary: The entry examines the focal question of what biological individuals are and why no single everyday definition settles it. Familiar organisms are clear starting points, but cases such as a genetically connected fungus, coral reefs, microbial communities, insect colonies, genes, species, and multispecies hosts complicate the picture. The authors distinguish a broad category of biological individual from the narrower category of organism. They also emphasize two major dimensions. Physiological individuals are functionally integrated metabolic wholes whose parts are coordinated and regulated. Evolutionary individuals, especially Darwinian individuals, are entities participating in heritable variation and differential reproduction across lineages. These dimensions can come apart: something may be a living, integrated whole without reproducing as an evolutionary unit, or it may be an evolutionary unit without being a living agent in the ordinary sense. Debates over microbialism, eliminativism, holobionts, group selection, and species-as-individuals show why organism-centered thinking can be both useful and limiting. Pluralists propose that several categories or models may be needed, depending on explanatory aims and biological practices. The entry also considers autonomous agency, life cycles, reproduction, and the regulation of cooperation and conflict. Finally, it presents the evolution of individuality as a contested history of transitions in which lower-level entities sometimes become parts of more integrated higher-level individuals.
key_ideas: The category biological individual may include organisms, parts of organisms, groups, lineages, and multispecies partnerships.
Physiological and evolutionary individuality are related but distinct. Functional integration does not automatically produce an evolutionary individual.
Organism-centered biology can overlook microbes, symbioses, genes, populations, and other possible individuals.
Holobionts and microbial communities motivate disagreement about whether individuality belongs to a host, its symbionts, the combined system, or several of these at once.
Pluralist views hold that different scientific purposes may justify different ways of individuating the same biological case.
The evolution of individuality concerns how previously separate entities become more integrated, regulated, and capable of forming higher-level lineages.
summaries.why_it_matters: The concept of individuality connects philosophical questions about categories and boundaries with biological questions about selection, symbiosis, development, and evolution. It affects how researchers describe organisms, microbiomes, colonies, species, and ecological systems. The topic also demonstrates a broader lesson about science: empirical discoveries can pressure existing concepts, while conceptual analysis can reveal which empirical facts are relevant. Rather than forcing every case into one definition, comparing physiological, evolutionary, developmental, and ecological perspectives can make biological explanations more precise.

important_terms.definition: A broad category for biological entities, including organisms, parts, and groups, whose boundaries and unity are investigated philosophically.
An individual identified by functional unity, metabolism, internal regulation, and cohesion among its parts.
An individual involved in a population where traits vary, are heritable, and influence reproductive success.
A living whole composed of a multicellular host and closely associated symbiotic organisms.
The use of more than one legitimate category or model for describing biological individuals.
A series of stages or events through which a living thing passes across generations.
The capacity of a biological system to regulate its activities and remain relatively independent of its surroundings.
A proposed mechanism that limits disruptive selection among an entity’s parts or preserves selection between entities.

questions_to_think_about: What evidence would show that a multispecies partnership is an evolutionary individual rather than a stable community?
Can one entity be a physiological individual without being a Darwinian individual?
Does choosing a scientific purpose change what exists, or only how scientists describe it?
Should species and clades count as biological individuals if they are historical lineages rather than living agents?
What kinds of cooperation and conflict help create a new level of individuality?

summaries.example: Imagine an aspen grove whose trees grow by cloning. Each visible tree can be counted as a separate plant-like unit, called a ramet. But all the connected trees may come from one original genetic individual, called a genet. So the answer to “How many plants are here?” depends on whether we are counting visible shoots or the larger genetic lineage. This does not mean counting is arbitrary; it means different biological questions may require different boundaries.
summaries.summary: The entry explores why “biological individual” is harder to define than it first appears. Animals, plants, and other familiar organisms seem like obvious individuals, yet biology also includes enormous fungi, coral reefs, microbial communities, genes, colonies, species, and lineages. These examples do not all have the same kind of unity. Some are integrated living systems with metabolism, internal regulation, growth, and self-maintenance. Others are important because they form lineages in which traits are inherited and reproductive success differs. The entry calls the first kind physiological individuality and the second evolutionary individuality. An organism is often both, but not always. For example, a multispecies partnership might function as one coordinated living system without reproducing as one evolutionary unit. The discussion of microbes challenges the habit of treating large, familiar organisms as the only important examples. The idea of a holobiont describes a host together with closely associated symbionts, but philosophers and biologists disagree about whether the host, its partners, the combined system, or more than one of these should be counted. A pluralist approach says that several kinds of individuality may be legitimate, especially when different research goals require different boundaries. The entry also links individuality to life cycles, agency, cooperation, conflict, and the evolution of new levels of organization.
key_ideas: The ordinary idea of an organism is an important starting point, but it does not cover every possible biological individual.
A large fungus or coral reef can challenge the assumption that one individual must have a simple, visible boundary.
Some philosophers emphasize physiological unity; others emphasize evolutionary reproduction and heritability.
Microbes and symbiotic partners show that organisms often depend on other living things.
Groups such as insect colonies, species, or clades may count as individuals in some evolutionary accounts, but this is debated.
Pluralism allows different concepts to answer different scientific questions without assuming that all concepts are interchangeable.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate matters because the way scientists draw boundaries influences how they study evolution, disease, ecosystems, reproduction, and cooperation. It can reveal hidden participants, especially microbes and symbiotic partners, and can prevent the assumption that every biological system has one obvious level of organization. Learning to compare competing definitions is also a useful philosophical skill: evidence matters, but so do the purposes and concepts used to interpret that evidence.

important_terms.definition: A biological thing, part, or group treated as one unit for a biological explanation.
A living, organized whole such as an animal or plant, though some groups may also be described this way.
An individual whose parts cooperate and are regulated as a functioning metabolic whole.
An individual involved in heritable variation and differences in reproductive success.
A view that there can be several useful and legitimate kinds of biological individuals.
A group of a multicellular organism and its associated symbiotic microbes.
A sequence of developmental stages that can connect one generation to the next.

questions_to_think_about: In the aspen example, is the ramet, the genet, or both a biological individual?
Why might a coral reef be considered a living whole but not an evolutionary individual?
Does dependence on microbes make an organism less individual, or does it reveal how individuality works?
When does a group become more than a collection of separate organisms?
Can a scientific concept be useful even when its boundaries are not perfectly sharp?
